specialist_findings.claim: Rate-limiting is explicitly deferred for the POC. The decision at G-5 acknowledges this with 'flagged for WS7 security-expert review', but the deferral means the API ships without rate-limiting even though it is bearer-gated and sits behind Cloudflare. Cursor integrity has no tamper-protection. G-5 explicitly opts out of HMAC-signing cursors on the grounds that 'tampering only affects the caller's own pagination'. For an authenticated internal API this is proportionate, but cursor parameters encoding datasetVersionId + sort tuple could be manipulated by a compromised or rogue internal caller to probe internal version identifiers or force out-of-band pagination states. The GIAS daily CSV endpoint is described as 'no auth, plain GET' and ingested over a public URL pattern (ea-edubase-api-prod.azurewebsites.net). The plan records the endpoint URL with a date-substitution template. If the date-stamped URL is predictable by a third party, and if the pipeline does not verify checksum/signature of downloaded content, a supply-chain substitution (DNS or MITM) could inject malicious source data that survives the hard-fail-validation layer unless field-level checks cover structure and not just presence. WS3 specifies checksum-based unchanged-source short-circuit but does not mandate TLS certificate pinning or response-body signature verification from the official source.

The split-token format embeds the id+secret in a single bearer value ('oak_sds_<id>_<secret>'). The plan specifies HMAC-SHA-256 + pepper hashing at rest and prefix-only logging. WS2.2 proposes surfacing `tos_uri` mapped to the cookie policy URL (https://www.thenational.academy/legal/cookie-policy). The plan treats the Codex Plugin Marketplace as an assumed submission target, citing its 2026-03-26 launch date. No evidence is held that the Codex marketplace has open third-party submission at the time of execution, that submission criteria have been published, or that a non-OpenAI entity can list a plugin with an external MCP server. specialist_findings.claim: Admin API is fully exported in the bundled release artefact (line 206-208: 'Keep admin API exported in the full surface; read-only access is enforced by API-key privileges, not package mutation'). This is a deliberate design choice but it means any consumer who obtains a privileged Elasticsearch API key can invoke admin operations via the same released tarball. Architectural principle says the surface should express intent; a separate admin subpath or a build-time strip of admin exports would make the privilege model explicit in the package surface, not only in key-scope docs.

The plan introduces two build lanes (monorepo unbundled vs. release bundled) managed by two separate tsup config files (lines 167-168: 'tsup.release.config.ts (new)'). There is no stated mechanism to keep both configs in sync as the SDK surface evolves. The risk row at line 342 acknowledges divergence risk and proposes test-backing, but no constraint (lint rule, CI diff check, or schema-level lock) is cited to enforce it. Drift between lanes is likely to surface silently until a downstream smoke test catches it.

The downstream consumption proof (WS2.4, line 244-257) is described as 'fully local (no network, no release upload required)'. This is appropriate for CI but it means there is no plan-level assertion that the artefact produced locally matches what gets uploaded by the CI release workflow. A tarball built on a developer machine and one built in CI can differ due to Node version, pnpm lockfile state, or environment variables. A deterministic build hash or reproducible-build check is absent from the plan.

The plan correctly defers npm publication (lines 93-94) and references the future promotion path via a related plan (lines 392-393). The GitHub release-asset lane is positioned as a temporary stepping stone, not a durable distribution channel. This is architecturally sound for the stated immediate need but the plan does not address what triggers the promotion gate, nor whether the GitHub-asset lane gets retired when npm publishing lands. A sunset or promotion trigger clause would complete the architectural story.

The `./retrieval` subpath export is planned at lines 131-135 and 203-204 but the plan does not define which types are excluded from the retrieval surface. Without an explicit type-level contract (e.g. a barrel that re-exports only retrieval types), the boundary is enforced only by documentation and key scopes. A stricter approach would be a separate entry point file that imports only retrieval symbols, making the surface mechanically verifiable.
